cards.b: Plants feed us, clean our air, give timber, medicines and fibres, and hold soil. Knowing how they are built and how water moves in them explains farming, irrigation and why forests matter for climate.

From simple to complex: bryophytes (mosses, no true vessels), pteridophytes (ferns, vessels but spores), gymnosperms (naked seeds: pine, cycas) and angiosperms (flowering plants, seeds in fruits). Angiosperms are the biggest group and split into monocots (one seed leaf, parallel veins) and dicots (two seed leaves, net veins).

• Roots: anchor, absorb water and minerals through root hairs.
  • Stem: holds leaves up, carries fluids.
  • Leaves: make food. Pores called stomata, opened by guard cells, let in CO2 and release water vapour and O2.
Xylem carries water and minerals up from roots (dead tubes). Phloem carries sugar from leaves to where it is used (living tubes).

cards.h: How water goes up a tall tree
cards.b: No pump pushes it. Water evaporating from leaves (transpiration) pulls a continuous column, held together by cohesion between water molecules, like a drinking straw. This is the cohesion-tension idea (Dixon and Joly, 1894). Root pressure helps a little. Phloem uses pressure-flow (Ernst Munch, 1930).

A flower is the reproductive organ. Pollen from the stamen lands on the stigma of the carpel and grows a tube to the ovule. Double fertilisation (found by Nawaschin and Guignard, 1898): one sperm makes the embryo, another forms the food tissue (endosperm). The ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes a fruit. Pollinators are bees, birds, bats and wind.

Auxin makes shoots bend to light (Darwin's 1880 coleoptile experiments; Went isolated auxin, 1928). Gibberellins make stems grow; cytokinins promote division; ethylene ripens fruit; abscisic acid closes stomata in drought. Day length controls flowering (photoperiodism).
Stephen Hales (1727) measured transpiration. Van Helmont's willow (1640s) hinted that plants gain mass from water. Barbara McClintock found jumping genes in maize (1940s, Nobel 1983).

Fix these

  • Roots do not 'suck' water; it is pulled up from above.
  • Not all plants have flowers.
  • Plants do not take food from soil, only water and minerals.

Birbal Sahni studied the fossil plant Pentoxylon and gymnosperms of Gondwana. J.C. Bose recorded plant movement. Ethnobotany, such as turmeric, neem, tulsi and the Ayurvedic plant stock, is part of daily life. Edavaluthu Kakkat Janaki Ammal (1897-1984), a plant cytogeneticist, worked on sugarcane and magnolias, and later led the Botanical Survey of India. India's Botanical Survey of India (1890) records about 55,000 plant species.

• Plant groups: bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms.
  • Xylem up (water), phloem down (sugar).
  • Transpiration pull draws water up.
  • Double fertilisation in angiosperms.
